claims.text: The proposed initial materials are homogenized equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloys such as NbMoTaW in a pristine solid state.
Combining high-temperature DSC with in situ dilatometry or high-energy X-ray imaging enables determination of melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting.
The combined method will determine these melting properties efficiently.
Using an inert argon atmosphere and heating rates below 10 K/min ensures thermal equilibrium during measurement.
Reference materials such as gold and alumina can standardize temperature and enthalpy measurements.
The in situ volume measurement can be synchronized with DSC acquisition.
DSC onset and completion signatures of melting can be correlated directly with real-time volume-change data.
DSC records endothermic or exothermic latent heat associated with melting and solidification.
Integration of baseline-corrected DSC peaks yields the enthalpy of fusion.
The entropy of fusion can be derived from the DSC-derived enthalpy using thermodynamic relations.
In situ dilatometry or X-ray imaging quantitatively tracks dimensional changes and thereby measures the volume change at melting.
The method will measure melting temperatures with an accuracy of ±1–2 K.
The method will determine fusion enthalpy and entropy with uncertainties of ±3–5%.
The approach is applicable across a broad compositional range of high-entropy alloys.
Conventional calibrated high-temperature DSC without in situ volume monitoring may rely on post-melting density measurements that miss rapid structural relaxation.
The approach is best suited to HEAs that remain chemically stable and single-phase at high temperatures.
Rapid phase decomposition or complex multiphase behavior limits the method unless measurement protocols are adjusted.
Instrument coupling, temperature-dependent calibration, and high-temperature nonequilibrium effects can introduce measurement uncertainty.
Verification against multiple standards is needed to establish reliability across different HEA systems.

The approach is to be rejected if melting temperature differs from benchmarks by more than ±2 K, fusion enthalpy or entropy differs by more than ±5%, or no volume discontinuity correlates with the DSC melting signal.
